title: The VGA CRT controller, its registers
covers: The CRT controller registers of the IBM VGA, reached through the index register at hex 03D4 and the data port behind it

rows.text: A data register is accessed by writing its index to the Address register at hex 03D4 or 03B4, then the data to the other port; the capture reads 0384.
The I/O address used depends on bit 0 of the Miscellaneous Output register; the figure writes the variable digit as a question mark.
Reserved bits must be preserved: read the register first and change only the bits required.
The Address register is at hex 03D4 or 03B4, the capture reading 0384 and 0304, and holds an index that points at a data register.
Bits 4-0 are the index of the data register reached through the port at hex 03D5, the capture reading 0305 or 0385.
The three high bits are set to 0 and undefined on read; the capture prints the zero as e.
The address port is read back as the whole stored byte, so bits 7-5 keep what was written to them.
A write of the data port is ignored while the VGA register lockout switch is on.
The whole stored byte is the index: bits 7-5 select the register too, not only bits 4-0.
Index values not listed in the register table are reserved.
A write to an unlisted index reaches no register the table defines.
DOSBox-X hands an unlisted index and the value to the SVGA write handler when one is installed, and otherwise logs an unknown index.
A read of an unlisted index goes to the SVGA read handler, or logs the unknown index and answers 0.
The Horizontal Total register (bits 7-0) holds the total number of characters in one horizontal scan interval, retrace time included.

A character counter counts the character clock, comparators compare the register value with the horizontal character width for horizontal timings, and all horizontal and vertical timings rest on this register.
A write stores the byte, which the document reads as the character total minus 5.
The Horizontal Display-Enable End register (bits 7-0) defines the length of the horizontal display-enable signal and the number of character positions per line.
A write stores the byte, which the document reads as the displayed character total minus 1.
A change calls VGA_StartResize, except when the ignore-smaller option is on and the new value is smaller, which logs instead.
The Start Horizontal Blanking register (bits 7-0) is the horizontal character count at which horizontal blanking becomes active.
A write stores the count at which the horizontal blanking signal becomes active.
The End Horizontal Blanking register determines when the horizontal blanking signal becomes active.
Bits 6-5 are the display enable skew control; it delays the display enable signal from zero to three character clocks.
Bits 4-0 hold the five low bits of a six-bit end blanking count; the most significant bit is bit 7 of index hex 05.
A write stores the low bits of the end blanking count that the start value and width W give.
The Start Horizontal Retrace Pulse register (bits 7-0) names the character position where the horizontal retrace signal becomes active, centring the screen.
A write stores the character position where horizontal retrace starts.
A write that changes the value sets the hretrace debug event flag.
Bit 7 is bit 5 of the end horizontal blanking value in the End Horizontal Blanking register at index hex 03.
Bits 6-5 skew the horizontal retrace signal by zero to three character clocks to centre the screen.
Bits 4-0 give the character count at which horizontal retrace becomes inactive; the width W is added to the start retrace value.
A write stores the byte whose low five bits end horizontal retrace, compared with the start retrace register.
The Vertical Total register (bits 7-0) holds the eight low-order bits of a 10-bit vertical total; bits 8 and 9 are in the Overflow register.
The vertical total is the number of horizontal raster scans including vertical retrace, minus 2, and it determines the vertical retrace period.
A write stores the low eight bits, which the document reads as the scan count minus 2.
A write that changes the value calls VGA_StartResize.
A write stores the byte that carries bit 9 of the vertical retrace start, of the vertical display-enable end and of the vertical total.
Bit 8 of the line compare, of the start vertical blanking, of the vertical retrace start, of the vertical display-enable end and of the vertical total live here too.
Bit 4 of the byte also sets bit 8 of the line compare before the read-only check, so it is stored even when read-only is on.
Bits 6-5 are the byte panning field, used in pel panning; Extended Graphics mode behaves as if they are zero, so programs should set them to 0.
Bits 4-0 are the starting row scan count for the row after a vertical retrace; the counter is cleared, not preset, at the maximum row scan.
The controller latches the start address at the start of vertical retrace, so these registers should be loaded during active display.
A write stores the byte panning in bits 6-5 and the starting row scan count in bits 4-0.
DOSBox-X also stores the low five bits as hlines_skip and, on a VGA, bits 6-5 as bytes_skip; other architectures store zero.
Bit 7 converts 200-line video to 400 lines: the row scan counter clock is halved and each line is displayed twice.
Bit 6 is bit 9 of the line compare and bit 5 bit 9 of the start vertical blanking.
Bits 4-0 give the number of scan lines per character row, the maximum row scan number minus 1.
A write stores the scan lines per row in bits 4-0 and the doublescan flag in bit 7.
On a VGA the write also puts bit 6 into bit 9 of the line compare; on an EGA it ignores bit 7.
DOSBox-X sets address_line_total to the low five bits plus one, doubles it when bit 7 is set, resizes on a change and sets the maxscan debug flag.
Bit 5 disables the cursor when set.
Bits 4-0 give the row within the character box where the cursor begins, the first cursor line minus 1; a value greater than the cursor end shows no cursor.
A write stores the cursor's first scan line in bits 4-0 and turns the cursor off with bit 5.
On a VGA DOSBox-X enables the cursor when bit 5 is clear and stores the low five bits as sline; other architectures enable it unconditionally.
Bits 6-5 are the cursor skew control, delaying the cursor by 0 to 3 character clocks.
Bits 4-0 give the row where the cursor ends; a value less than the cursor start shows no cursor.
A write stores the cursor's last scan line in bits 4-0 and its skew delay in bits 6-5.
DOSBox-X stores the low five bits as eline and bits 6-5 as delay.
The Start Address High register (bits 7-0) holds the 8 high-order bits of the 16-bit start address of the regenerative buffer.
The start address points to the first address after vertical retrace, latched at its start, so the registers should be loaded during active display.
A write stores the high eight bits of the start address.
DOSBox-X marks the display to be drawn again and folds the byte into bits 15-8 of display_start.
The Start Address Low register (bits 7-0) holds the 8 low-order bits of the start address of the regenerative buffer.
A write stores the low eight bits of the start address.
DOSBox-X marks the display to be drawn again and folds the byte into bits 7-0 of display_start.
The Cursor Location High register (bits 7-0) holds the 8 high-order bits of the 16-bit cursor location.
A write stores the high eight bits of the cursor location.
DOSBox-X folds the byte into bits 15-8 of the cursor start address.
The Cursor Location Low register (bits 7-0) holds the 8 low-order bits of the cursor location.
A write stores the low eight bits of the cursor location.
DOSBox-X folds the byte into bits 7-0 of the cursor start address.
The Vertical Retrace Start register (bits 7-0) holds the low eight bits of the 9-bit vertical retrace start, in horizontal scan lines; bit 8 is in the Overflow register.
A write stores the low eight bits of the vertical retrace start.
Bit 7 protects CRT controller registers at index 00 through 07 from writes; the line compare bit in the Overflow register is not protected.
Bit 6 selects five memory refresh cycles per horizontal line instead of three and should be 0 for supported operations.
Bit 5 enables a vertical retrace interrupt, IRQ2, when clear; check the CRT interrupt bit to see whether the video raised it.
Bit 4 clears a vertical retrace interrupt when clear; the handler clears then sets it to reset the flip-flop.
Bits 3-0 end vertical retrace, compared with the vertical retrace start; the width W is added to the start value.
A write stores the byte holding the protection, refresh, interrupt and retrace-end fields.
On a VGA DOSBox-X stores bit 7 as the read-only lock; clearing bit 4 clears the trigger, and on an EGA deactivates IRQ 9.
The Vertical Display-Enable End register (bits 7-0) holds the 8 low-order bits of a 10-bit value defining the display-enable end; the two high bits are in the Overflow register.
The 10-bit value is the total number of scan lines minus 1.
A write stores the low eight bits of the value the document reads as the scan line total minus 1.
A change resizes the screen; a change under 3 lines is delayed 150ms after removing the pending resize.
The Offset register (bits 7-0) gives the logical line width; the next character row's start address is 2 or 4 times the value further.
A write stores the line width, counted in word or doubleword addresses.
DOSBox-X sets the low bits of the scan length from the value, rechecks the scan length, and a change sets the scanstep debug flag.
Bit 6 makes memory addresses doubleword addresses.
Bit 5 clocks the memory-address counter with the character clock divided by 4, used with doubleword addresses.
Bits 4-0 give the horizontal scan line of a character row where an underline occurs, the desired scan line minus 1.
A write stores the underline scan line and the doubleword and count-by-4 bits.
A write also rechecks the address shift and the scan length.
The Start Vertical Blanking register (bits 7-0) holds the low bits of a 10-bit value where vertical blanking becomes active.
Bit 8 of that value is in the Overflow register and bit 9 in the Maximum Scan Line register; the value is the scan line count minus 1.
A write stores the low bits of the blanking start, which the document reads as the scan line count minus 1.
A change calls VGA_StartResize.
The End Vertical Blanking register (bits 7-0) gives the horizontal scan count where vertical blanking ends, in units of a scan line.
For a blanking width W, W is added to the start vertical blanking value minus 1 and the low bits are programmed.
A write stores the low bits of the end blanking count that the start value and width W give.
A change calls VGA_StartResize.
Bit 7, cleared, disables the horizontal and vertical retrace signals; set, it enables them, and it resets no other register.
Bit 6 selects word mode when clear and byte mode when set; the doubleword bit in the Underline Location register also controls addressing.
Bit 5 selects MA15 or MA13 for the output pin in word mode; in odd/even mode it should be set.
Bit 3 gives the address counter the character clock divided by 2; bit 2 divides the horizontal retrace clock by 2.
Bit 2 selects the clock for the vertical timing counter: the horizontal retrace clock or that clock divided by 2.
Dividing the retrace clock doubles the vertical resolution to 2048 scan lines, the vertical total being 10 bits wide.
Bit 1 selects the source of output bit 14 and bit 0 the source of output bit 13: the row scan counter's bit or the address counter's.
The Color/Graphics Adapter's controller used 128 scan-line addresses; for 640-by-200 VGA programs 100 scan lines with two addresses per row.
A write stores the reset, word/byte, address wrap, count, retrace select and row scan select fields.
DOSBox-X also derives the Tandy line mask, shift and address mask from the low bits and rechecks the address shift and scan length.
The Line Compare register (bits 7-0) holds the 8 low-order bits of the 10-bit compare target; reaching it clears the line counter's start address.
That split screen keeps the lower screen immune to scrolling; bit 8 is in the Overflow register and bit 9 in the Maximum Scan Line register.
A write stores the low eight bits of the compare target.
